title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2023)
problem_statement: Analyzes the economic and computational inequities caused by subword tokenizers in commercial language model APIs that charge per token, demonstrating that low-resource languages incur higher monetary costs and latency overhead for identical semantic content.
domain: Natural Language Processing, Subword Tokenization, NLP Economics & Fairness
theoretical_framework: Cross-lingual tokenizer fertility analysis and pricing policy critique for token-based commercial NLP billing models.
methodology: Empirically measures token fertility, byte-to-token ratios, monetary cost per task, and generation throughput across 22 typologically diverse languages using commercial API tokenizers (including OpenAI tiktoken cl100k_base, text-davinci-003, and Cohere) on standardized translation datasets.
evaluation: Relative cost ratio compared to English
key_findings: Commercial tokenizers exhibit severe cross-lingual fertility disparities, requiring up to 6x more tokens to represent equivalent semantic content in low-resource languages compared to English.
Because API pricing models charge uniformly per token, speakers of low-resource languages pay significantly higher financial costs for identical linguistic tasks.
High subword fragmentation dilutes semantic token embeddings and limits the effective context length available for multi-sentence reasoning in under-represented languages.
Language-agnostic Byte-Pair Encoding trained predominantly on English web text allocates fewer subword merges to non-dominant languages, forcing character-level fallback.
scope_and_delimitations: Focuses on commercial API tokenizers and pricing models across 22 languages spanning high-resource, medium-resource, and low-resource tiers on parallel corpora.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Our analysis is limited to 22 languages selected based on data availability in FLORES-101, and does not assess dialectal variations, informal social media slang, or mixed-language code-switching.
limitations.summary: The analysis focuses on standard translated text across 22 languages and does not evaluate informal social media dialects, code-switched text, or morphological affixes in agglutinative hybrids.

generalizability_gap: Evaluated on clean standard language benchmarks; does not cover code-switched social media text (such as Tagalog-English Taglish) or domain-specific emergency disaster microblogs.
methodological_gap: Does not measure joint multi-task gradient conflict or sequence labeling degradation induced by token over-fragmentation during fine-tuning.
future_work: Designing equitable tokenizer pricing structures based on semantic content or byte length rather than subword token count.
Exploring adaptive cross-lingual tokenizers tailored for multilingual and low-resource deployment.
